en: 1.1 Thus have I heard.
1.2 At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī,
was at war with the Vṛjis.
1.3 He thus addressed these words to the assembly.

"I shall destroy these Vṛjis—prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants; I shall annihilate them and bring about their ruin through injustice."
1.4 Then King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, ruler of Magadha, addressed Varṣākāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha.
1.5 Come, Varṣākāra, approach the place where the Blessed One is.

"Having approached, pay homage with your head at the feet of the Blessed One in our name, and inquire after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, ease of movement, vigor, strength, well-being, blamelessness, and his state of dwelling in comfort."
1.6 (And speak thus:)
King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, has come into conflict with the Vṛjis.
He speaks these words in the assembly thus:
"I [shall establish] these Vṛjis— prosperous, flourishing, secure,
well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people."
I shall destroy; I shall annihilate.
"I shall bring about his ruin through misconduct.
[The Blessed One asked: "What do you mean by this?"
Just as the Blessed One, Vārṣākāra, explains it, so should you grasp it.
For what reason? Because:
For the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones do not speak untruthfully.
1.8 “‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ replied Varṣākāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, to King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha; having given his assent,
[he brought] a all-white mare.”
Having mounted his chariot,
surrounded by a group of young brahmins and carrying a golden staff, he departed from Rājagṛha in order to visit the Blessed One in his presence.
...for the purpose of attending upon him.
Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground would allow for the vehicle, he alighted from the carriage and ascended Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa on foot.
He approached the Blessed One, and having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One face-to-face, and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the brahmin Varṣākāra [addressed] the brahmin-minister of Magadha...
Then the Blessed One said this to him.

1.10 (King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One and inquires after his freedom from illness, his freedom from affliction, and— ) as before, up to— his dwelling in comfort.
1.11 "May King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha, Varṣākāra, and yourself be happy.
1.12 "Venerable sir, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha has come into conflict with the Vṛjis."
He thus addresses these words to the assembly:
"I shall devastate these flourishing, prosperous, secure, well-supplied, and densely populated Vṛji territories; I shall destroy them and bring about their ruin through injustice."
1.13 (“What does the Blessed One Gautama say?
1.14 (“Varṣākāra, there was once a time when I was dwelling among the Vṛjis in the country at the Cāpāla shrine.”)
In that regard, I have taught the Vṛjis the seven qualities that prevent decline.

"Varṣākāra, as long as the Vṛjis continue to undertake and practice these seven qualities that prevent decline, and as long as these seven qualities that prevent decline are observed among the Vṛjis, one may expect only the increase of the Vṛjis' wholesome qualities, not their decline."
"1.15. Thus, venerable sirs, I do not understand the detailed meaning of what was spoken in brief and without analysis by this Blessed One Gautama."
May the Blessed Gautama explain in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief.
"In this way, I shall properly understand the detailed meaning of what has been spoken in brief by the Blessed One Gautama, which was not yet analyzed.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Blessed One.
Fanning the one possessing cows.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, have you heard that the Vṛjis hold frequent assemblies and dwell with great frequency of assembly?
"I have heard it, Bhadanta, that the Vṛjis hold frequent assemblies and dwell with great frequency of assembly."

1.19 “Furthermore, Varṣākāra, as long as the Vṛjis meet frequently and dwell with great frequency of assembly, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected for the Vṛjis, not decline. 1.20 “Have you heard, Ānanda, that the Vṛjis assemble in full council, rise from their meeting in full council, and perform the duties of the Vṛjis in full council?”
1.21 "Venerable sir, I have heard that the Vṛjis assemble together, rise up together, and perform their Vṛji duties together.
1.22 "And as long as, Varṣākāra, the Vṛjis will assemble together..."
“If they rise up [from their practice], and if they perform the duties of the Vṛjis in unison, then only growth for the Vṛjis is to be expected regarding wholesome qualities, not decline.

“Have you not heard, Ānanda, that the Vṛjis do not resolve what has not been resolved, nor do they abandon what has been resolved; they proceed by undertaking and following the Vṛji-dharma as it has been prescribed?”
1.24 "Venerable sir, I have heard that the Vṛjis do not resolve upon what is not resolved upon,
nor do they abandon what has been resolved upon; they proceed by undertaking and abiding in the Vṛji-dharma as it has been prescribed."

1.25 "Furthermore, Varṣākāra, as long as the Vṛjis do not make new vows that have not been made, nor do they abolish vows already made, but continue to abide having undertaken the Vṛji-dharma as it has been prescribed— for them, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline. 1.26 "Have you heard, Ānanda, that those Vṛji-ladies, the daughters of the Vṛjis, and the Vṛji-maidens were protected by their fathers?"

[They are] girls protected by their mother, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their father-in-law, protected by their mother-in-law, protected by their kinsmen, protected by their clan, accompanied by legal sanctions, having a master, accepted by another,
or even those merely encircled by a garland; [they are] such as these.
They do not, by force or violence, rush forward and engage in conduct regarding sensual pleasures.
"Venerable sir, I have heard that the Vṛjis are those who [practice] the Vṛji-dharma."
Even kings and Vṛji maidens— those protected by their fathers, protected by their mothers, and so forth as previously described, even those girt with flower garlands— even such women as these do not,
having suddenly and forcibly assailed them, fall into misconduct regarding sensual pleasures.

1.28 And as long as, Varṣākāra, the Vṛjis, the Vṛji-lords, and the Vṛji-maidens— as previously described, down to those even encircled by garlands— do not, out of passion, suddenly and by force intrude upon such women and engage in sexual conduct, there will surely be growth.
"There shall be no decline in the virtuous qualities expected from the Vṛjis.
"Ānanda, have you heard anything about the Vṛjis?
Those who are the Vṛjis—the Vṛji mahallakas—honor them, revere them, respect them, and worship them; they consider their word to be worthy of being heard."
1.30 “I have heard, venerable sir,
that those Vṛjis who honor, revere, respect, and worship the elders of the Vṛjis consider their words worthy of being heard.
1.31 “And as long as, Varṣākāra, the Vṛjis will honor, revere, respect, and worship those elders of the Vṛjis, they will listen to their words.”
They will think: "Only the increase of wholesome qualities is to be expected for the Vṛjis, not their decline."

1.32 “Ānanda, have you heard that the Vṛjis— those who revere, honor, respect, and worship the Vṛji shrines located in the four directions of the Vṛji territory, and do not abolish their ancient traditions and practices?
1.33 “I have heard it, Bhadanta, that the Vṛjis— those who revere, honor, respect, and worship the Vṛji shrines located in the four directions of the Vṛji territory.”
Thus they do not abolish their ancient customs and traditions.
1.34 And as long as, Varṣākāra, the Vṛjis honor those Vṛji shrines that are located in the four directions of the Vṛjis...
They will revere, honor, respect, and worship [them]; and their ancient signs and conduct will not be cut off.
Indeed, an increase of virtues and wholesome qualities is to be expected for them.
There is no falling away.

1.35 “Ānanda, have you heard from the presence of the Arhats of Vṛji whether a keen mindfulness of protection has been established, such that future Arhats might come, and those who have arrived might find delight and not be deprived of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick?”
With medicines and requisites that are not conducive to faith.

1.36 “Venerable sir, I have heard in the presence of the Vṛjis, who are Arhats, that a protective mindfulness is established with intense mental application: ‘May future Arhats come here, and may those who have already arrived find delight;
and may they not be deprived of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.’”
1.37 And as long as, Varṣākāra, an intense mindfulness of protection is maintained toward the Arhats, [thinking]:
"May the Arhats who have not yet arrived come, and may those who have already arrived find delight? [so long shall it be.]
And may they not be deprived of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; rather, an increase in wholesome qualities and no decline is to be expected for the Vṛjis.

1.38 "And as long as, Varṣākāra, the Vṛjis continue to practice by undertaking these seven principles that prevent decline, and as long as these seven principles that prevent decline are observed among the Vṛjis, only growth for the Vṛjis is to be expected, not the decline of wholesome qualities. 1.39–1.40 "Furthermore, O Gautamas, if the Vṛjis were endowed with even a single one of these factors, they would be invincible to King Māgadha Ajātaśatru."
If this is true for the son of Vaidehī, what need is there to mention him with all [his qualities]?
"Come now, Gautama, we shall depart; we have many duties and much to do."
1.42 "Varṣākāra, you may now consider it the time."
1.43 Then Varṣākāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
2.1 Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda.
"Summon all the monks who dwell depending on Vulture Peak Mountain to the assembly hall.
"So be it, Venerable Sir."

The venerable Ānanda, having assented to the Blessed One, gathered together all the monks who were dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain and brought them into the assembly hall; he then approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side,
the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
2.3 "Venerable sir, as many bhikṣus as there are dwelling in dependence upon Vulture Peak Mountain, they have all assembled in the assembly hall."
"Now, if the Blessed One deems it the right time. Then the Blessed One went to the assembly hall.
Having approached, he sat down on the very seat prepared in front of the community of monks.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks.
2.5 "Monks, for seven days I shall teach you the qualities that do not lead to decline. Listen to them, and attend to them well and thoroughly; I shall speak."
What are the seven factors conducive to decline?
Monks, as long as you dwell in frequent assemblies and remain devoted to frequent gatherings, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected for the monks, not decline.

2.7. Monks, as long as they will assemble in harmony, rise from their assembly in harmony, and perform the communal duties of the Saṅgha in harmony, only growth and not decline in the wholesome qualities of the monks is to be expected. 2.8. And as long as the monks do not make a vow for what is aimless (*apraṇihita*), nor shall they cut off that which has been vowed, [so shall it be].
Having undertaken the training in the prescribed rules, the increase of the monks is to be expected.
There is no falling away from the qualities of a śrāvaka.

2.9 And as long as monks do not fall under the power of craving— which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and passion, and finds enjoyment here and there— only growth, monks, is to be expected for wholesome qualities, not decline.
2.10 (And furthermore, monks,
those monks who are elders, knowers of the night, long-ordained... [they] will honor, revere, respect, and worship them.
They will accept their words as a stream [of authority], and for those monks, only the increase of wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.
2.11. "And as long as, monks, [the monks] shall dwell in remote lodgings in forest retreats and wilderness regions, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected for the monks, not decline.
2.12. "And as long as, monks, [the monks] shall [behave] toward their fellow practitioners of the holy life..."

“With a focused mind, mindfulness for protection is established: ‘May fellow practitioners of the holy life who have not yet arrived come; may those who have already arrived find delight; and may they not be deprived of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick. One should expect only the increase, and not the decline, of the monks’ wholesome qualities.
As long as the monks shall abide having undertaken these seven factors that prevent decline among the monks...”
And when these seven qualities that do not lead to decline are observed, an increase— and not a decrease— of the monks' wholesome qualities is to be expected.
2.14 (I shall also teach you seven other qualities that do not lead to decline; listen to them, attend well and thoroughly to them, and I will speak.)
What are the seven qualities that do not lead to decline?
2.15 And as long as, monks, they will honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Teacher;
and having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped the Teacher, relying upon him, they will dwell;
and they will honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Dharma, the training, the instruction, heedfulness, hospitality, and concentration.
Having honored, revered, respected, worshipped, and relied upon this samādhi, they will dwell [in it]; for those monks, only an increase in wholesome qualities is to be expected,
not a decline.
2.17 Furthermore, I shall teach you seven other qualities that do not lead to decline. Listen to them well, pay close and careful attention, and I will speak.
What are the seven qualities that do not lead to decline? (2.18) Monks, as long as you do not become fond of worldly activity, fond of talk, or fond of sleep...
He does not [engage in] communal recitation... [he does not... vi-...
With the attainment of the remainder,
[and] the internal cessation... monks should expect only an increase in wholesome qualities, not a decline.
2.19 Only in Tib.
2.20 (I shall teach you seven other qualities that are not to be abandoned; listen to them, attend to them well and thoroughly, and I shall speak.)

What are the seven qualities that prevent decline? (2.21) Monks, as long as you will be faithful, possessed of a sense of shame, conscientious, energetic, established in mindfulness, concentrated, and wise, only an increase in monks in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not a decrease.
2.22 Only in Tib.
2.23: "I shall also teach you seven other qualities that do not lead to decline; listen to them well, attend to them thoroughly and properly, and I will speak."
What are the seven qualities that do not lead to decline?
(2.24) Monks, as long as they are knowers of the Dharma, knowers of the meaning, knowers of the proper time, and knowers of moderation...

"O you who know yourselves, who know the assembly, and who know the superior and inferior among individuals—for such monks, only the increase of wholesome qualities is to be expected, not their decline.
"I shall teach you seven other qualities that prevent decline; listen well and attend closely, and I will speak."

What are the seven qualities that do not lead to decline? (2.27) Monks, as long as they cultivate the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness— which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment— and likewise the factors of enlightenment that are the investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity;

(They will cultivate that which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment; for these monks, only an increase in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not a decline.
2.28 (And as long as, monks, the monks shall abide having undertaken these seven qualities that prevent decline...)

And the seven qualities that prevent decline will be seen; for the monks, only an increase in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not a decline. (2.29) "Monks, I shall teach you the six qualities that inspire affection. Listen to them, attend well and thoroughly, and I shall speak."

What are the six qualities that inspire affection? (2.30) "Toward the Teacher, my bodily action will be established as friendly... [and so forth]. Toward wise persons... [and so forth]. Toward companions in the holy life... [and so forth]. Toward those who have entered the path... [and so forth]. Toward those who have not yet entered the path... [and so forth]. Toward all sentient beings... [and so forth]. What are the six qualities that inspire affection? They are: being endowed with faith, being endowed with ethical discipline, being endowed with learning, being endowed with generosity, being endowed with wisdom, and being endowed with loving-kindness. These are the six qualities that inspire affection. What are the six qualities that inspire respect? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire respect. What are the six qualities that inspire fearlessness? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire fearlessness. What are the six qualities that inspire trust? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire trust. What are the six qualities that inspire delight? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire delight. What are the six qualities that inspire joy? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire joy. What are the six qualities that inspire confidence? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire confidence. What are the six qualities that inspire reliance? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire reliance. What are the six qualities that inspire veneration? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire veneration. What are the six qualities that inspire honor? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire honor. What are the six qualities that inspire reverence? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire reverence. What are the six qualities that inspire worship? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire worship. What are the six qualities that inspire service? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire service. What are the six qualities that inspire attendance? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire attendance. What are the six qualities that inspire following? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire following. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation in others? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation in others. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation in both oneself and others? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation in both oneself and others. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation in the assembly? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation in the assembly. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation in the community? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation in the community. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation in the world? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation in the world. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation among gods and humans? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation among gods and humans. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation among the noble ones? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation among the noble ones. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation among the wise? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation among the wise. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation among those who dwell in the forest? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation among those who dwell in the forest. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation among those who practice alms-gathering? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation among those who practice alms-gathering. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation among those who wear rag-robes? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation among those who wear rag-robes. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation among those who dwell at the foot of a tree? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation among those who dwell at the foot of a tree. What are the six qualities that inspire emulation among those who dwell in the open air? They are: being learned, being one who has heard much, being a retainer of what has been heard, being a preserver of the Dharma, being skilled in the meaning, and being skilled in the letter. These are the six qualities that inspire emulation among
Nor [should one speak ill] of fellow practitioners of the holy life.

This Dharma is delightful, pleasing, venerable, and agreeable; it leads to affection, reverence, respect, cultivation, gathering, concentration, freedom from strife, freedom from dispute, and to one-pointedness of mind.
2.31 Friendly verbal action; 2.32 friendly mental action;

2.33 whatever righteous gains there may be, obtained in accordance with the Dharma—even down to those placed in the bowl or contained within the bowl—in such gains we shall be partakers of common enjoyment, not enjoying them in secret.
Together with wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
This Dharma is conducive to affection, as before.

2.34 By means of those ethical disciplines which are unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, liberating, unadulterated, well-perfected, properly undertaken, praised by the wise, and not censured by the wise— by such ethical disciplines as these, we shall come to share in the commonality of virtue together with the wise, [being] with them...
by those who practice self-restraint.
This Dharma is delightful, as before.

2.35 This noble view is leading to liberation, penetrative, and leads forth to the complete destruction of suffering and the making of an end to suffering by means of that which effects it; through such a view, we shall come to share the same perspective as our wise fellow-celibates.
This Dharma is delightful, as previously described, up to: it conduces to unification of mind.

2.36. "Monks, as long as monks continue to undertake these six principles of cordiality, and as long as the six principles of cordiality are observed among the monks, only growth— and not decline— of the monks' wholesome qualities is to be expected."
2.37 (Nur Chin. (Uddāna here in Tibetan) 3.1 (Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:)
"Come, Ānanda, let us go to Pāṭaligrāmaka.
"Very well, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, wandering on tour through the Magadha country together with the community of monks, stayed one night at Rājāgāraka between Pāṭaligrāma and Rājagṛha,
near a bamboo thicket.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, it is because of the lack of knowledge, the lack of vision, the lack of realization, and the lack of penetration regarding the four noble truths that I and you have wandered and transmigrated through this long course of time.
Which four? [They are:
suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
"Due to lack of knowledge, lack of vision, lack of understanding, and lack of penetration, I and you have wandered and transmigrated through this long course of time."
3.5 This noble truth of suffering has been penetrated and thoroughly understood.
The path to existence has been destroyed; the cycle of birth is exhausted; now there is no further becoming.
3.6 The noble truth of the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been penetrated; it has been thoroughly understood and eradicated.
The conduit to existence is exhausted; the cycle of birth has ended; now there is no further becoming.
3.7 Only in the Tibetan version.
3.8 Because of not seeing the four noble truths as they truly are.
I and you have wandered through this long course of saṃsāra;
those truths have now been seen.
The conduit of existence has been uprooted.
"The cycle of birth is exhausted;
now there is no further existence. Thereupon, the Blessed One [addressed] the Venerable Ānanda...
He addresses [them] with these words.
Come, Ānanda, let us go to Pāṭaligrāmaka.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Magadha country, arrived at Pāṭaligrāmaka and stayed there at the Pāṭalaka shrine.
4.3 The yakṣas, brahmins, and householders of Pāṭaligrāma heard [this].
The Blessed One Gautama, while wandering on a tour through the Magadha country, arrived at Pāṭaligrāma and stayed there at the Pāṭala shrine.

But that jar into which those bones have been placed, please give it to us,
so that we may [dispose of them] in Droṇagrāmaka.
"Having established a stūpa for the relics of the Blessed One,
we shall hoist parasols, banners, and flags; we shall offer a great procession and honor, revere, respect, and venerate [it] with perfumes, garlands, flowers, incense, and musical instruments."
We shall conquer.
51.7 “So be it,” Varṣākāra, the chief minister of Magadha, replied to the brahmin of the Dhūmra clan.
51.8 Then the brahmin of the Dhūmra clan divided the relics of the Blessed One into eight portions.
51.9 Then the brahmin of the Dhūmra clan gave one portion to the Mallas of Kuśinagara, [saying: “By which [Kuśinagara]...”
The Malla citizens of Kuśinagarī were establishing a stūpa for the Blessed One’s body,
raising parasols, banners, and flags, and offering great processions with perfumes, garlands, flowers,
and incense.
From the beginning,
they treat [them] with respect, revere them, honor them, and worship them.
51.10 He assigned the second portion to the Mallas of Pāpā, so that the Mallas of Pāpā might establish the stupa for the Blessed One’s body at Pāpā.
As before, up until they worship.

He assigned a third portion to the *calakalpaka* *bulakas*, so that the *calakalpaka* *bulakas* might establish the stūpa for the body of the Blessed One at Calakalpā and worship it, as described previously, up until the point of their making offerings.
He bestowed a fourth portion upon the brahmins of Viṣṇudvīpa, so that the brahmins of Viṣṇudvīpa might establish a stūpa for the Blessed One’s body in Viṣṇudvīpa,
[and] as before, up until they worship it.
He bestowed a fifth share upon the Krauḍyas of Rāmagrāma, so that the Krauḍyas of Rāmagrāma might establish a stūpa for the Blessed One’s body in Rāmagrāma;
[the account continues] as before, up until they pay homage to it.

He bestowed a sixth share upon the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, by means of which the Licchavis of Vaiśālī erected a stūpa for the relics of the Blessed One in Vaiśālī, and as before, up until they paid worship to it.
51.15 He bestowed a seventh share upon the Śākyas residing in Kapilavastu, so that the Śākyas of Kapilavastu might establish a stūpa for the Blessed One’s relics in Kapilavastu,
and [perform] all the rites up to their worship, as previously described.

He granted an eighth share to Varṣākāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, by means of which King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha established a stūpa for the Blessed One’s relics at Rājagṛha,
hoisted parasols, banners, and flags, and offered a great procession with perfumes, garlands, and flowers.
He honors, respects, reveres, and worships [them] with incense and musical instruments.

51.17 But the jar into which those bones have been cast, they present to a brahmin of the Dhūmra lineage; by means of that, the brahmin of the Dhūmra lineage establishes a jar-stūpa at Droṇagrāmaka, as previously described, up until he worships it.
51.18 At that time,
the young brahmin Pippalāyana was seated and present in that assembly. 51.19 Then the young brahmin Pippalāyana said this to the Mallas of Kuśinagara:
51.20 “Listen, sirs, Mallas of Kuśinagara, whether you be assemblies, guilds, corporations, or councils!”
For a long time,
that state of existence has been dear to us, even though it was shrouded in darkness.
And it was pleasing to the mind.
He has passed into final nirvāṇa in your village field.
We deserve a portion of the relics of that Blessed One.
Now, from among the bodies that have been divided, may you give us those embers by which [you] shall construct an ember-stūpa for the Blessed One.
I shall establish [this] parasol of Gautama at Pippalavatī.
And I shall hoist victory banners and dispatch a great procession with perfumes.
"I shall honor, revere, respect, and worship [him] with garlands, flowers, incense, and music.
The people of Kauśinagara offer [these things].
[They gave] coals of the bodies to the young Brahmin Pippalāya,
by which the young Brahmin Pippalāya...
In Ippalavatī, he establishes a stūpa for Aṅgara,
hoists parasols, banners, and flags, and dispatches a great procession with perfumes, garlands, flowers, incense, and musical instruments.
He will honor, revere, respect, and worship [them].
At that time,
there were eight reliquary stupas of the Blessed One in Jambudvīpa, the ninth being the urn stupa and the tenth the charcoal stupa.
51.23 This is the natural law in this regard.
Therefore, this is said:
"Of the eight *droṇas* of the relics of the Visionary One in Jambudvīpa, seven receive worship."
And a single Droṇa [of relics] of the Supreme Person is worshipped by the Nāga king in Rāmagrāma.
Of the Supreme Person’s four tusks,
one tusk is worshipped in the world of the thirty gods.
The second [was] in the delightful city of Gandhāra;
the third [was] in the conquered territory of the Kaliṅga king.
The tusk of the Supreme among Men is worshipped by the Naga king in Rāmagrāma; this is the fourth [relic].
